title: Frost & Ice
strapline: A morning when the whole garden has turned white and glittery overnight — and it will not last, so come and look now.
intent: A frosty morning is a fleeting piece of magic children rarely get to study — provision that seizes it turns a cold day into real, first-hand science.
Watching ice melt in warm hands, frost vanish in the sun and puddles turn solid overnight introduces change of state as something felt long before it is named.
Freezing, cracking and melting invite genuine investigation: what melts fastest, what stays frozen in the shade, how to free a treasure trapped in ice.
Cold, glittering frost and slippery ice sharpen the senses and grow careful, observant looking.
Children connect the season to what they see — it froze because it was so cold last night, the sun is melting it now — early cause and effect in the natural world.
Wintry words arrive with the wonder — frost, frozen, melt, slippery, sparkle, crack, thaw.
implementation: Get out early on a frosty morning, before it goes, and simply look — frost furring the leaves, ice skinning the puddles, breath in clouds.
Offer warm hands and dark and sunny spots to test: 'Which frost will disappear first — the bit in the sun or the bit under the bush?'
Freeze things overnight on purpose — ice with berries or small toys inside, ice in different-shaped tubs — and set children the puzzle of freeing or melting them.
Model the wondering: 'It was water yesterday and now it's hard as glass — what happened to it in the night?'
Bring in gentle maths and sequence — which melts first, second, last; time an ice cube with a sand timer; sort what's still frozen from what has thawed.
Record the change: photograph the frozen puddle at breakfast and again after lunch, and talk about what the sun did while you were busy.
key_questions: Which frost will disappear first — the bit in the sun or the bit under the bush?
It was water yesterday and now it's hard as glass — what happened in the night?
How could we free the treasure trapped in the ice?
Which melts first, second and last?
What did the sun do to the frozen puddle while we were busy?

impact.text: Children meet change of state first-hand — ice melting, frost vanishing, puddles turning solid overnight.
Children investigate what melts fastest and what stays frozen — genuine testing of cause and effect.
Children connect the season to what they see — it froze because it was cold, the sun is melting it now.
Children sequence and time the melting, sorting what's frozen from what has thawed.
Children gain wintry words — frost, frozen, melt, slippery, sparkle, crack, thaw.

enhancements: Treasures frozen into ice overnight for children to free and melt.
Warm hands and sunny and shady spots to test where frost goes first.
A sand timer to race melting ice cubes.
Before-and-after photos of the frozen puddle at breakfast and after lunch.
Ice frozen in different-shaped tubs to compare how they melt.

playing_exploring: Children explore cold, frost and ice with hands and eyes, chasing a wonder that is here one hour and gone the next.
They test what happens when ice is warmed, moved into the sun or left in the shade.
active_learning: Children persist at real problems — melting the ice to reach the toy trapped inside — and see them through.
creating_thinking: Children predict which ice will melt first and check it, linking the cold night and the warm sun to what they see.
